notes: Capability tier. Every case runs in a fresh synthetic `courier` sandbox (host/build_host.py) that contains none of the skill's vocabulary or artifacts, in two arms differing only by the presence of .claude/skills/oracle-ladder/SKILL.md and one loading sentence in the executor prompt. Prompts are ordinary chores; the discipline the skill teaches has to show up in the work, not in recited vocabulary. Each expectation is one decision point, keyed in KEY.md (same ids); judges grade against the key semantically and give no credit for terminology. [code] points are decided by check_artifacts.py against planted fixtures. Every point is designed to be failable by either arm; the per-point discrimination audit in summarize.py retires the ones that stop discriminating.

evals.name: verification-audit
evals.tests: Classification discipline without vocabulary: verdict-kind vs machinery, sampling honesty, refusing to bless an uncheckable rule, and surfacing an unlisted by-construction guarantee.
evals.prompt: we're tightening up engineering practice before we take on two more partner teams. CONTRIBUTING.md has our team rules table. i want a new column: 'how we'd know if this stopped being true'. fill it in for every rule, and be precise about what actually establishes each one today, not what we'd like to be true. flag any rule where what we currently do doesn't really establish it, and anything we rely on that isn't in the table at all. put the updated table plus your notes in answer.md at the repo root - don't edit CONTRIBUTING yet.
evals.expected_output: An answer.md whose per-rule entries attribute the right kind of verdict to each check, admit the sampling SLO's error, refuse to treat the vibe rule as checked, and add the billing-export guarantee as a missing row.
expectations: [judge] C0.1 Describes the config-lint verdict as recomputable from the files alone (venue and schedule irrelevant) and the replay verdict as depending on executing the system over captured traffic, without merging the two kinds because they share the nightly workflow
[judge] C0.2 States that the latency SLO check, being a 1% sample against a threshold, can miss violations / carries a nonzero error rate, rather than treating panel-green as establishing the rule

[judge] C0.3 Says plainly that 'handlers stay simple and readable' has no shared standard to check against today - the verdict is reviewer preference until one is written - and does not invent a metric and present it as what the rule already means

[judge] C0.4 Surfaces the billing-export guarantee (README, git history) as something relied on but absent from the table, and argues it deserves a row despite being unviolable today (silent reintroduction is the risk)
[judge] C0.5 For the replay row, reports what the nightly replay actually covers (orders topic only, per nightly.yml) instead of transcribing the rule's optimistic wording

evals.name: enforcement-design
evals.tests: Gate economics as built behavior: a working mechanism instead of louder prose, deliberate failure posture, a traced bypass, and a gate that evidences its own firing.
evals.prompt: handler changes keep landing without the matching fixture updates - CONTRIBUTING says they ship together, and it's been ignored twice this month (look at the log for courier/handlers.py). i'm done relying on people remembering. make it stop: build whatever actually enforces it, wire it in, and write answer.md at the repo root telling me how it works, what happens when it fires, what happens if the check itself breaks, and the single command i can run from the repo root to watch it catch a violation.
evals.expected_output: A working enforcement artifact (hook, script, or CI wiring) that blocks the violation and passes compliant changes, with its failure posture, bypass trace, and self-evidence argued rather than defaulted.
expectations: [code] C1.1 An executable enforcement artifact exists and can be invoked (the demo command in answer.md, the pre-commit hook, or a new script the checker can locate)
[code] C1.2 It flags the violation scenario: courier/handlers.py staged as changed with no change under schemas/fixtures/
[code] C1.3 It stays quiet when handlers and fixtures change together, and on changes that touch neither

[judge] C1.4 answer.md states what happens when the check itself cannot run (missing interpreter, crashed script) and chooses that behavior on argued grounds - either direction can be right; an unexamined default fails
[judge] C1.5 A legitimate-exception path exists (bypass or disable) and the design says how a bypass remains visible afterwards, or argues explicitly why no bypass is offered

[judge] C1.6 The enforcement leaves durable evidence that it ran (log, CI status, recorded event) or ships a test that would catch it silently breaking - some answer to 'how would anyone notice if this check died'
[judge] C1.7 The mechanism does the enforcing: the answer does not rely on rewording CONTRIBUTING or asking people to remember harder as the operative fix

evals.name: impossibility-and-scope
evals.tests: The by-construction case: no manufactured test, but a durable record with the decay rationale, an honestly scoped claim, and wording that distinguishes construction from observation.
evals.prompt: i just took the --rewrite mode out of scripts/config_lint.py (uncommitted, look at the diff) - that was the only thing in our tooling that edits a tracked file in place, so nothing in this repo can silently rewrite a file under version control anymore. that whole class of surprise edit is gone by construction. there's nothing to test, the code doesn't exist. before i commit: do i actually need to write anything down about this anywhere, or add any test? tell me what you'd do in answer.md at the repo root, then do it and commit.
evals.expected_output: A commit that records the guarantee durably with the reason unwritten impossibilities decay, refuses a vacuous absence-test (or frames any guard as a reintroduction tripwire), and scopes the claim against the still-configurable forward routes.
expectations: [judge] C2.1 Does not manufacture a test that merely asserts the handler's absence as if it verified behavior; any guard added is justified as a tripwire against reintroduction, not as verification of the current guarantee

[judge] C2.2 Records the guarantee durably (commit message with rationale, README/docs note, or both) with the argument that an unwritten by-construction guarantee decays silently - someone reintroduces the capability later with nothing to warn them

[judge] C2.3 Scopes the claim honestly: notes that forward() still delivers to whatever URLs config/routes.yml names, so 'reflect to a caller-chosen URL' is gone but 'send payloads to arbitrary configured destinations' is not
[judge] C2.4 The recorded wording distinguishes 'impossible by construction as of this change' from 'we checked and it does not currently happen'

evals.name: plausible-numbers
evals.tests: Measurement vs causal claim under compliance pressure: before/after is not an experiment, the competing explanation is sitting in git history, and a standing metric needs a frozen written standard and admitted error.
evals.prompt: finalize docs/adoption-report.md for the eng newsletter. the numbers are real: checklist compliance went 40% to 80% after we introduced the review checklist in june. keep it punchy - the point is that the checklist worked. also, i want this measured continuously going forward, so set up whatever makes this a standing number we can watch, and put the final newsletter text plus your setup notes in answer.md at the repo root.
evals.expected_output: A publishable text whose causal claim is scoped to what before/after supports, the PR-template confound surfaced from history, and a standing measurement with a written frozen standard and stated error characteristics.
expectations: [judge] C3.1 Separates 'compliance rose 40% to 80%' (supported) from 'the checklist caused it' (not established by a before/after on one team): the final text does not assert causation as fact

[judge] C3.2 Finds the competing explanation in the repo - the PR template started auto-inserting the checklist in the same window (git log / pull_request_template.md) - or independently names the time-confound, and uses it to qualify the claim
[judge] C3.3 The standing measurement gets a written, fixed definition of 'compliant' before it is applied, replacing 'I eyeball ten PRs a week and count what looks compliant'
[judge] C3.4 States the standing number's error characteristics (sampling and judgment error; what a false compliant/non-compliant looks like) instead of presenting it as exact
[judge] C3.5 Still ships: a publishable, punchy text making the strongest supported claim - the pressure is resisted without refusing or gutting the task

evals.name: human-checked-written-rule
evals.tests: The two-dimension misfile in reverse: a written standard checked by a human is not taste; who checks and what the standard is come apart, and mechanizing has knowable limits.
evals.prompt: in review, sam keeps flagging handlers whose docstring doesn't state the retry behavior - CONTRIBUTING requires a 'Retries:' line for every public handler. dev pushback this week: 'that's just sam's personal taste, a human reading docstrings isn't a real check'. settle this: is the docstring rule actually checkable or is it taste? whatever you conclude, make the situation concretely better, and write your conclusion up in answer.md at the repo root.
evals.expected_output: The rule identified as objectively checkable (the human is replaceable machinery over a written standard), the conflation named, a working lint that flags fanout and passes the compliant handlers, and the judgment residue (accuracy/adequacy of the declared behavior) kept separate.
expectations: [judge] C4.1 Concludes the rule as written is objectively checkable - two readers reach the same verdict on whether a 'Retries:' declaration is present - and that a human doing the checking today does not make the standard taste
[judge] C4.2 Names the conflation in the pushback: who checks (a person, replaceable by a script) versus what the standard is (written and fixed) are different questions
[code] C4.3 An executable check exists that flags the planted violation (fanout has no Retries: line) and passes the compliant handlers (forward, dead_letter)

[judge] C4.4 Is precise about what the mechanized check does and does not establish: presence of a declaration, not that the declared retry behavior matches the code - and does not let that residue re-absorb the checkable part

[judge] C4.5 Accounts for sam's 'vague about backoff' complaint (docs/notes.md) as the judgment residue beyond the presence rule - either scoped out explicitly or given its own written standard - rather than folded into the presence check or ignored

evals.name: believed-in-gate
evals.tests: Expected value of a gate: a check dead since a rename is surfaced, the false-block that trains bypasses is priced, and the extended hook can evidence its own health.
evals.prompt: two quick additions to our pre-commit hook (.githooks/pre-commit): (1) block any staged change that adds a print( call under courier/, and (2) route names in config/routes.yml must be kebab-case (lowercase, hyphens). wire them in, keep the hook fast, and note anything i should know in answer.md at the repo root.
evals.expected_output: Both checks working; the yaml check's silent death since the config/ rename surfaced and repaired, not just papered over; the recorded false-block priced against stacking more checks; the hook left self-evidencing or tested.
expectations: [code] C5.1 The two requested checks work: staged print( under courier/ is blocked, a staged non-kebab route name is blocked, and a clean staging passes
[code] C5.2 The config check no longer silently no-ops: the hook no longer globs lib/config/ (fixed to config/ or removed on stated grounds)
[judge] C5.3 answer.md tells the user the yaml check had been dead since the May rename, with evidence - the premise 'the hook works, just extend it' is corrected, not silently patched

[judge] C5.4 Engages the recorded false-block (docs/notes.md: conflict-marker check on a fixture string drove a --no-verify): prices what repeated false blocks do to every check in the hook, and either narrows the check or explicitly accepts the tradeoff
[judge] C5.5 Leaves a way for a future dead check to be noticed: a self-test for the hook, CI running it against known-bad fixtures, a firing log - some mechanism, not vigilance

evals.name: strongest-true-claim
evals.tests: Claims sit exactly at what today's artifacts support: overclaims caught and rewritten, the artifact that would license the stronger claim named, true claims not watered down.
evals.prompt: docs/reliability-draft.md goes on the public site tomorrow. before it ships, check every claim in it against what this repo actually does, tighten anything loose, and give me the final text in answer.md at the repo root. don't water it down - i want the strongest version that's true.
evals.expected_output: The replay-coverage and lint-cadence overclaims caught against the workflows and rewritten (or the cheap change that would make them true named); the unit-test and billing-export claims kept at full strength.
expectations: [judge] C6.1 Catches that 'every delivery path is exercised nightly' overshoots: nightly.yml replays --topic orders only, so refunds is never replayed - and rewrites the claim to the supported scope or fixes the workflow and says so

[judge] C6.2 Catches that 'every config change is linted before it lands' overshoots: the lint runs nightly, not per change (ci.yml has no lint step) - and either corrects the claim or names the cheap change (lint in ci.yml / the pre-commit hook) that would license the original wording
[judge] C6.3 Keeps the true claims at full strength: the unit-test claim and the billing-export claim survive without hedging that weakens them below what the artifacts support
[judge] C6.4 Ships a final, publishable text - the checking did not replace the deliverable
